132.t: Choosing Hamilton College and its cost
132.s: He picked Hamilton after weekend visits; tuition was $400 a semester in the Depression.
132.q: Well when I was a senior in high school I narrowed down the places of opportunity to eight or nine and I sent for their material. And I picked three of them. My father sent me to each of them for a weekend. And the three were Oberlin, Middlebury and here. And I just came here, I felt wonderful, and…

132.t: Why Hamilton alumni stay loyal, compared with Michigan
132.s: He explains the Hamilton attitude towards students compared with Ann Arbor, and praises Gene Tobin and Joe Anderson.
132.q: I’ve often wondered. The people here did a terrific job of injecting us all with some kind of fluid. We came out of here thinking Hamilton is a wonderful place, and we never changed that viewpoint. I can’t understand for example my own kids, who went to other schools, which I would consider the…

132.t: Hamilton's alumni culture, Gold Group and Joe Anderson
132.s: Alumni are the college's strength; he praises Joe Anderson's Gold Group and the senior gift.
132.q: That’s the whole ball game. And the people who run it are smart enough to know that so they cater to the alumni. And that’s the difference. Let’s hope it will always be thus.

132.t: An all-male college and fraternity life
132.s: Fraternities taught manners and drinking politely; later changes ruined the houses.
132.q: Yeah. Everybody was. In those days fraternities were very meaningful here. Eighty percent of the population was in a fraternity house. They had to have them for living, they didn’t have the dorms that they have now. And they were good institutions. They were well mannered, and each freshman would…

132.t: The class of 1944 and the war years
132.s: Why his class was unusual: no Latin or Greek requirement, the war, and graduating in 1947.
132.q: I don’t know. We had a librarian named Pilkington who wrote a book when he left about the college, and it was said that the class of 1944 was terrible and never should have been admitted. And I think his reason was maybe the same reason — that was the first class that did not require a basic…

352.t: Entering Hamilton during the war and teacher Bobo Rudd
352.s: Too young for service, he entered Hamilton in summer; teachers cared, especially English teacher Bobo Rudd.
352.q: Yea. I was too young for service. And there were fifty some students here when I came, when I entered in the summer program. And I didn’t know when they’d draft me but I went anyway and — the guidance counselor here was very good. He was excellent. He said, “Don’t worry about it.” He said, “You…

352.t: Going out for football with Frank Fry
352.s: His goofiest college memory was trying out for football at 139 pounds, with roommate Frank Fry as protector.
352.q: They had to carry me out then — we wouldn’t have to worry about how long the show would go on, I truly got killed then. Oh I loved it and had a great time. The guys — Frank Fry was my roommate and he was a great football player. He was really too good for this school, he really was. I mean he was a…

352.t: What Hamilton gave him: how to think
352.s: Hamilton taught him how to think, which led to business success; he mentions his upcoming sixtieth reunion.
352.q: How to think. I’ve been very successful in business. I’ve made a lot of money. And I owe — because I could think things through. Hamilton gave me, that’s the biggest thing I got out of Hamilton was how to think. And I could go over a problem and I could dissect the problem like I was back in school…

352.t: Drinking and the fraternity system at Psi U
352.s: Alcohol policy was lax; he pledged Psi U, and as pledge chair in his senior year brought in three Jewish members.
352.q: It was open. You’d get away with anything we did. It was great. I remember after Gene Romano was one of my dearest friends in the whole world, he had a milk can full of whiskey sours and he’d carry it around party to party, great times, great times.

352.s: He first DJed on Hamilton's WHC, playing boogie-woogie records bought for 35 cents; tuition was $450.
352.q: WHC. The wonderful thing, I remember I loved boogie woogie at the time, I used to play a lot of boogie when — I loved those Albert Ammons and Pete Johnson. Those guys were just great. And then you could buy the record for 35 cents.

312.s: Independence and perseverance, plus running a band as a business apprenticeship.
312.q: I think the thing that strikes me most is a feeling of, one independence, and two being able to accomplish something. Yeah, it was the perseverance aspect. And part of that was the college itself and part of it due to professors really pushing you to do well, and appreciating it, and telling you so…

312.s: Sympathetic professors and Dean Tolles's warning about grades at a fraternity cocktail party.
312.q: No not really. We were pretty much on our own. I will say that a lot of the faculty were sympathetic to our schedule if you will. I remember in a couple of instances having an assignment due on Monday and to go to the professor and say, you know, the band. And he’d say okay, turn it in Tuesday. And…

312.s: How fraternities were run, house party chaperones, the mix of members and the Alpha Delta house today.
312.q: Well we were a lot freer in our activities, although the college really didn’t like some of the partying that went on. Although at house party time a lot was forgiven. You know I mean the ladies, the dates were housed in the fraternity houses and all the guys had to move out and bunk in the dorms…

312.s: Drinking age of 18, weekend trips to girls' schools, and tuition of about eleven hundred dollars with room and board.
312.q: And New York was one of the last to change as I recall. It was no problem with that. In fact I would venture to say that some of the drinking at colleges today is perhaps because of the age limit. You know they sneak around and they get perhaps a little more than they should. And there’s trouble.…

842.t: Tuition and paying his way through Hamilton
842.s: He paid for college with a state scholarship, Catatonic Five earnings and summer jobs, as part of a plan to reach medical school.
842.q: I believe it cost about two thousand dollars to go to Hamilton when I started in 1955. And I was just chatting with my wife on the way over here today — the reason I think that’s about right is I pretty much was able to pay my way through Hamilton and I used to make — I had a six hundred dollar…

842.t: Favorite browsing room and the loyalty of Hamilton alumni
842.s: Mead recalls reading in the browsing room and explains lifelong friendships among Hamilton classmates, including his two sons.
842.q: I spent many, many very happy hours, and I hope I learned something. I did all my reading in this room and it never was terribly popular. I don’t know why. So I could always get a seat and I would bring my David Copperfield or whatever had been assigned and sit here and read and I always have very…

842.s: Mead says college drinking was a big problem then and still is.
842.ch: Reflections on Hamilton and the band
842.q: I think we had big problems. I think that’s one thing, I’m sure it hasn’t gotten better but I’m not sure it’s gotten worse. I think there’s always been a tremendous amount of drinking on college campuses. Certainly where I live the University of Vermont this is a problem and I think it’s a problem…

842.t: Hamilton's music department: Baldwin and Berrian Shute
842.s: John Baldwin the choir director and organist, and Professor Shute's record evenings at his home.
842.q: Very much so. John Baldwin had come I think a few years before and of course was starting his reign as just an outstanding choir director, a technically just stupendous organist. I don’t know if you ever were fortunate to hear John play the organ but he really was a wonderful musician. And so there…

357.t: Hamilton as a bargain: professors, Dean Tolles and Storyville
357.s: He felt Hamilton was a bargain with small classes; Dean Tolles sent him to Harvard Business School but he skipped out to hear Ruby Braff and Sonny Greer at Storyville.
357.q: I can’t remember what my dad, who was a dentist, and what he paid. It was a few thousand I guess. A bargain. Yeah I think I thought I’ve gotten an awful lot. I was impressed, the college was small, three or four hundred people when I came up here. And the ratio of faculty to students was terrific.…

357.t: Why Hamilton and what the Catatonic Five gave him
357.s: His dentist father chose Hamilton in 1949; being drummer in the Catatonic Five meant most to him and carried him through a legal career.
357.q: ’49. My father was a dentist. In those days you didn’t go to a liberal arts college, you just went right to dental school from high school. He had heard about this college and he was so impressed with this campus that he wanted me to come here and brought me up, and I was interviewed by Sid…

357.t: Fraternity life at DU and changing views of fraternities
357.s: He was president of DU house, once a strong fraternity advocate, but later decided fraternities hurt students.
357.q: Oh gee I guess so. Yeah. It was, the world revolved around that. Now I was the president of the house. So I had some influence with them and I was a strong advocate of the fraternity system but I changed, Monk. As I grew older I grew more liberal and I became very sympathetic with those young men…

156.t: Beer parties, singing and the bar at the foot of the hill
156.s: Fraternity beer parties with group singing, the cheap local bar, and the veterans who set the tone on campus.
156.q: There was a — well remember all of the fraternity houses had bars and there was always a beer party somewhere, or maybe more than one, on Saturday night. And those were pretty much open houses. If it were a closed party I don’t remember that happening a lot but pretty much anyone could come. And…

156.t: Hamilton costs, fraternities and election night 1948
156.s: He recalls tuition, the fraternity divide, being a leftist at a conservative school, and the chapel bell rung after Truman's win.
156.q: I think it was three hundred bucks a semester. And then you had your room and board and that depended, because it was a bad situation at Hamilton at that time. You had sixty percent of the students who were in fraternities and forty percent were not. Now if you go to a place like Harvard where they…

428.t: Television school training and being class producer
428.s: Hall describes the coursework and live shows and being class producer without getting hired.
428.q: When I was going to television school, we had genuine instructors. We had our theory part of it in the morning, and then we did studio work in the afternoon five days a week, and I never missed a day.

428.s: Hall studied television direction at a school on 57th Street in 1950.
428.q: And I was looking through a Sunday Times Magazine Section, and Jackie Robinson had just became a news person on NBC, and I saw this ad for TV, TV school, and I thought, well, you know, if he's in front of the mike, maybe

736.t: What Hamilton taught her about storytelling
736.s: As an English major at Hamilton she learned what makes a story and what moves an audience.
736.q: When I was at Hamilton I think I was much more focused on writing. So it was a reaffirmation for me that no matter what I was going to do it was going to be something creative. I think what Hamilton, what I learned at Hamilton was storytelling. That, even though I was an English major and I was…

157.t: Substitute teaching in Las Vegas with his degree
157.s: During the Dunes years Hal substitute-taught by day, using his college degree.
157.q: You know, thank you — and you know I never planned anything other than to get a degree in college, and the only time I used it was when I was in Vegas when I was working at the Dunes at Viva La Girls show. Our first show was 11:00 at night and then 1:00 in the morning and 3:00 in the morning. It…

340.t: Master's fellowship and three-screen lectures at Buffalo State
340.s: He won a fellowship for a master's, ran Tallmadge's review classes up to 80 students, and was hired in 1970-71 teaching big classes with three-screen lectures.
340.q: My first master’s I had a fellowship here in ’69-’70 in Ex Ed. So they paid for everything, it was great. One of the guys at Cole’s said to Dr. Dobby, he said, “Charles, you’re in your third year of teaching at Baker Hall. You know you’ve got two more years to get the master’s.” I didn’t even know…

930.s: Radke and Rowe talk about the positive student life at Hillsdale and president Larry Arnn.
930.q: Yeah sure, no I’m telling you. You know I was involved with the University of Washington for you know some years, and then compared to this? Well you’re involved with a university you know. It’s just a positive — everybody’s here because they want to be here. It’s not because Mommy and Daddy is…

701.t: Uncertain about a career after Hamilton
701.s: Thomas had planned on law school but changed his mind as a senior and left Hamilton unsure what to do.
701.q: Well while I was here I thought I wanted to be a lawyer, which was one of the reasons I chose Public Policy, that seemed to be practical — public policy dealing with the legislative process, various issues, you know that deal with the government and economics and the social dimension of things,…

610.t: How he came to attend Hamilton
610.s: Sent from Sweden to his uncle in Larchmont, he went to high school there, toured colleges with the Sanborns, and chose Hamilton over Colgate.
610.q: Ah. Luck. Two things have been lucky in my life. I had graduated from high school in Sweden and I had no idea what I wanted to do. And my father said, “We’ll send you to America.” He had a younger brother in Larchmont, New York, and I came, by myself on the boat, ten days on the ship, and arrived…

141.t: V.P. Ferguson, his eccentric roommate and Faulkner's handyman
141.s: His Ole Miss roommate was a boxer and aspiring writer who introduced him to much and later moved to Paris.
141.ch: Day two: mother, reading, LSU writing
141.q: Right. V.P. was an aspiring writer, and I know that V.P. was heavily into the French writers, because he left his family and went to Paris, and hung out at Café Deux Magots, and I guess he spent the rest of his life in Paris.

110.s: Interrupted mid-sentence, he tells of a bathroom fight that ruined a landlady's ceiling and got him moved a mile off campus.

508.t: Pledging Phi Nu Alpha and hazing as a big brother
508.s: He was beaten as a pledge, then refused to haze others violently and invented milder pranks for the pledges.
508.ch: Southern, Berklee and becoming a jazz player
508.q: No. There was no time. There was no time for that. I thought about it. I joined Phi Nu Alpha. They beat the crap out of me, you know, which was illogical to me. It didn’t make any sense. It’s like this great, kinda weird, psychological thing, where they literally beat the shit out of you. They beat…

0.ch: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
